explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - Cleanlab is an open-source Python library for data-centric AI. It provides a programmatic API (no standalone frontend) that lets users detect and correct data and label issues in ML datasets, and train noise-robust models. Its main use cases include dataset issue detection (Datalab), label-error detection (CleanLearning), data valuation, outlier detection, and task-specific extensions (classification, regression, segmentation, etc.).

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level directories:
     • cleanlab/           ← Core library code
     • docs/               ← Documentation site source (Sphinx)
     • tests/              ← Unit and end-to-end tests
     • .github/            ← CI workflows, issue/pr templates
     • configuration files: setup.py, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, .pre-commit-config.yaml, mypy.ini
   - Within cleanlab/:
     • classification.py, count.py, data_valuation.py, filter.py, rank.py, outlier.py  
     • datalab/            ← High-level “Datalab” class and issue-finding engine  
     • internal/           ← Core algorithms and utilities (knn_graph, metrics, numerics, validation)  
     • models/             ← Integrations with Keras and other frameworks  
     • task-specific subpackages: object_detection, segmentation, token_classification, multilabel_classification, regression  
     • experimental/       ← Example and prototype scripts
   - Tests mirror this structure under tests/ to validate each component.

3. Readme insights
   - User-facing API surface: CleanLearning, Datalab, dataset.health_summary  
   - Enumerates supported tasks and external frameworks (scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace, etc.).  
   - Shows a workflow: user supplies data & model, calls find_issues(), lab.report().

4. Components & interactions for the system diagram
   a. Main components:
      • User API Layer  
        – cleanlab.classification.CleanLearning  
        – cleanlab.Datalab  
        – cleanlab.dataset.health_summary  
      • Core Engine  
        – internal algorithms: confident-learning, rank-pruning, knn_graph, metrics, data valuation, outlier detection  
      • Task-Specific Modules  
        – classification, multilabel, token_classification, regression, segmentation, object_detection  
      • Adapter/Integration Layer  
        – models/keras.py and data adapters (e.g., imagelab)  
      • External ML Frameworks  
        – scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace, XGBoost, JAX  
      • Documentation & Testing  
        – docs/ Sphinx build pipeline, tests/ suite  
   b. Relationships & Data Flow:
      1. User code calls API Layer →  
      2. Core Engine orchestrates:
         • Preprocessing & data checks (internal/util)  
         • Task-specific issue detection (issue_manager)  
         • Algorithmic modules (knn_graph, numerics)  
      3. Adapter layer converts user data & model outputs into internal formats  
      4. Outputs returned to user (lists of issues, cleaned labels, robust model predictions)  
   c. Architectural patterns & principles:
      • Modular layering: clear separation between API, core algorithmic modules, and adapters  
      • Plugin/extensibility: each ML task has its own subpackage implementing a common interface  
      • Single responsibility: internal modules handle specific algorithmic concerns (graph construction, metrics, validation)  
      • Test-driven design: tests mirror code structure to ensure coverage  
   d. Key technologies & frameworks:
      • Python 3.8+  
      • NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn  
      • Optional: PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, JAX for model outputs  
      • Sphinx for docs, GitHub Actions for CI

5. Guidelines for an open-source library diagram
   - Emphasize the core functional pipeline (API → Engine → Adapters → External Frameworks)  
   - Show where new task-specific modules plug in (e.g., object_detection, segmentation)  
   - Illustrate how internal utilities are shared across modules  
   - Highlight the test and documentation workflows as supporting components  

6. Diagram drafting instructions
   - Draw boxes for each component:
     • API Layer  
     • Core Engine  
     • Task Modules (grouped)  
     • Adapter/Integration  
     • External Frameworks  
     • Docs & Tests  
   - Use directional arrows:
     • From user code to API Layer  
     • API Layer → Core Engine → Adapters → External Frameworks  
     • Core Engine → Task Modules  
   - Color-code by layer:
     • Blue for API  
     • Green for Core Engine  
     • Orange for Task Modules  
     • Gray for Adapters  
     • Yellow for External Frameworks  
     • Light gray for Docs & Tests  
   - Label arrows with data types (features, pred_probs, labels, issues, robust_model)

7. Detail emphasis
   - Label each module with its path (e.g., cleanlab/datalab, cleanlab/internal/neighbor)  
   - Show shared utilities (e.g., knn_graph) as a single box with multiple incoming arrows  
   - Capture the extensibility points where new tasks or adapters can be added

By following this outline, the system design diagram will clearly communicate how Cleanlab’s API and internal architecture collaborate to detect data issues, integrate with any ML framework, and remain extensible and testable. Ensure every component, arrow, and label is explicit to capture the library’s modular, layered design. 
</explanation>
